agree.reason: Dana gets her own $600K figure back, a break-even she can check in her head, a low-risk one-site start and a direct answer on the IT director, so she would plausibly take a 20-minute call, though the evidence base is thin.

honest.reason: The email turns the brief's blanket 'cut errors in half' into 'more than half' at one customer and shows the weaker 2.8→2.2 result too, but it leaves out that only two of six customers have shared data, and 'That's the problem we solve' overreaches a little.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out the $75,000 annual cost for five sites and the roughly 12% break-even against $600K, then measures both results (54% and 21%) against that bar, which is the most useful form these facts can take.

right_comparison.reason: Doing nothing means the $600K-plus a year in returns keeps going, and the email sets that cost against the software's price; the brief gives no trend to add.

qualification.reason: It names a real condition ('if your returns cost moves with your error rate') and offers a one-site trial she can check, but the trial has no time frame, target number or consequence if the target is missed.

objections.reason: It meets the IT director's likely resistance head-on: the software sits on top of the warehouse system, setup takes three weeks, and it offers a walkthrough before anything goes ahead, without raising objections the facts don't support.

fit.reason: At about 200 words in short paragraphs it reads easily on a phone, and it ends with a single clear request, as the brief asked.
